## 4. Graph Operations

Jafari, Alikhani, and Bakhshesh [15] propose investigating the behavior of the $k$ -coalition number under graph operations. In this section, we show that the $k$ -coalition number is superadditive under the graph join and (strictly) subadditive under the disjoint union. When the $k$ -coalition partitions of $G$ and $H$ are structured “nicely,” we can compute exactly the $k$ -coalition number of $G\sqcup H$ in terms of $\COk(G)$ and $\COk(H)$ .

We first show that the $k$ -coalition number is superadditive under the graph join.

#### Proposition 4.1.

Let $k\geq 1$ and let $G$ and $H$ be graphs each having at least $k$ vertices. Then

$$ \COk(G+H)\geq\COk(G)+\COk(H). $$

#### Proof.

Fix maximum–cardinality $k$ -coalition partitions of $G$ and $H$ , say $\mathfrak{X}_{G}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{\COk(G)}\}$ and $\mathfrak{X}_{H}=\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{\COk(H)}\}$ , respectively. We will show that $\mathfrak{X}_{G}\cup\mathfrak{X}_{H}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $G+H$ . By Observation 3.1, there are no $k$ -dominating sets in $\mathfrak{X}_{G}$ or $\mathfrak{X}_{H}$ . Suppose $X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathfrak{X}_{G}$ are coalition partners. Since neither $X_{1}$ nor $X_{2}$ can $k$ -dominate $V(G)$ , neither set $k$ -dominates $V(G+H)$ . Since the union $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ $k$ -dominates $V(G)$ , it follows that $|X_{1}\cup X_{2}|\geq k$ . Since every vertex in $V(H)$ is adjacent to every vertex in $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ , the union $k$ -dominates $V(H)$ and therefore forms a $k$ -coalition in $G+H$ . By analogous reasoning, every $k$ -coalition pair in $\mathfrak{X}_{H}$ is also a $k$ -coalition pair in $G+H$ . Thus, $\mathfrak{X}_{G}\cup\mathfrak{X}_{H}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $G+H$ and $\COk(G+H)\geq|\mathfrak{X}_{G}\cup\mathfrak{X}_{H}|=\COk(G)+\COk(H)$ . ∎

In fact, when we repeatedly take the join of a graph $G$ with itself, the $k$ -coalition number increases linearly with the number of vertices in $G$ . We begin by proving a more general statement.

#### Theorem 4.2.

Fix $2\leq k<n$ . Given $m\geq 2$ (possibly distinct) $n$ -vertex graphs $G_{1},G_{2},\dots,G_{m}$ , we have

$$ \COk(G_{1}+\dots+G_{m})\geq(m-1)n-k+2. $$

#### Proof.

First suppose that $G_{1},\dots,G_{m}$ are all $n$ -vertex cliques. Since the join of cliques is a clique, we have $G_{1}+\dots+G_{m}=K_{mn}$ . By Lemma 3.2, $\COk(G_{1}+\dots+G_{m})=mn-k+2\geq(m-1)n-k+2$ .

Now suppose that some $G_{i}$ is not a clique, which we may relabel to be $G_{1}$ . Then there exist two vertices $v_{1},v_{2}\in V(G_{1})$ that are nonadjacent. Pick a subset $X_{1}\subseteq V(G_{1})$ with $|X_{1}|=k$ , $v_{1}\in X_{1}$ , and $v_{2}\notin X_{1}$ . Then $X_{1}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set of $G_{1}+\dots+G_{m}$ (since $X_{1}$ does not $k$ -dominate $v_{2}$ ), but $X_{1}$ does $k$ -dominate $V(G_{1}+\dots+G_{m})\setminus V(G_{1})$ . Pick $X_{2}\subseteq V(G_{2})$ such that $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ is a $(k-1)$ -dominating set but not a $k$ -dominating set of $G_{1}+\dots+G_{m}$ (it may be that $X_{2}=\emptyset$ ). Note that $|X_{2}|\leq k-1$ . For each $u\in V(G_{1})\setminus X_{1}$ , pick a distinct $u^{\prime}\in V(G_{2})\setminus X_{2}$ (which we may do since $|V(G_{2})\setminus X_{2}|\geq|V(G_{1})\setminus X_{1}|$ ), and set $Y_{u}=\{u,u^{\prime}\}$ . Note that $\{u,u^{\prime}\}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ . Every singleton $\{v\}\nsubseteq X_{1}\cup X_{2}\cup\{Y_{u}\mid u\in V(G_{1})\setminus X_{1}\}$ , forms a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ . Therefore, the following is a $k$ -coalition partition of $G_{1}+\dots+G_{m}$

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{X}=\left\{X_{1}\cup X_{2}\right\}\cup\left\{Y_{u}\mid u\in V(G_{1})\setminus X_{1}\right\}\cup\left\{\{v\}\mid v\notin(X_{1}\cup X_{2}\cup\{Y_{u}\mid u\in V(G_{1})\setminus X_{1}\})\right\} $$

and so

$$ \COk(G_{1}+\dots+G_{m})\geq|\mathfrak{X}|=|V(G_{1}+\dots+G_{m})|-|V(G_{1})|-|X_{2}|+1\geq(m-1)n-k+2.\qed $$

#### Corollary 4.3.

Fix $k,n,m\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $2\leq k<n$ and $m\geq 2$ . For any $n$ -vertex graph $G$ ,

$$ \COk(mG)\geq(m-1)n-k+2, $$

where $mG=G+\dots+G$ denotes the join of $G$ with itself $m$ times.

It turns out to be much harder to prove that the $k$ -coalition number is strictly subadditive under the disjoint union. To obtain an upper bound, we start with an arbitrary maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition and then carefully move vertices between sets without decreasing the size of the partition. We require the following lemma.

#### Lemma 4.4.

Fix $k\geq 2$ . Given a non-empty collection $\mathcal{D}=\{D_{1},\dots,D_{n}\}$ of disjoint $k$ -dominating sets of a graph $G$ , there is a collection of non-empty disjoint sets $\pi=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{m}\}$ such that every $X_{i}\in\pi$ forms a $k$ -coalition with some $X_{j}\in\pi$ , $\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}=\bigcup_{j=1}^{m}X_{j}$ , and $|\pi|>|\mathcal{D}|$ .

#### Proof.

We may assume that $D_{1},\dots,D_{n-1}$ are minimal $k$ -dominating sets of $V(G)$ . If not, then there exists some minimal $k$ -dominating set $D_{i}^{\prime}\subset D_{i}$ . We replace $D_{i}$ with $D_{i}^{\prime}$ and add all vertices of $D_{i}\setminus D_{i}^{\prime}$ to $D_{n}$ . Since $|D_{i}|\geq k\geq 2$ , we may partition each minimal $k$ -dominating set $D_{i}$ into two $k$ -coalition partners $X_{i,1}$ and $X_{i,2}$ . If $D_{n}$ is not minimal, then there exists a minimal $k$ -dominating set $D_{n}^{1}\subseteq D_{n}$ , split it into $X_{n,1}^{1}$ and $X_{n,2}^{1}$ , and replace $D_{n}$ by $D_{n}^{\prime}=D_{n}\setminus D_{n}^{1}$ . Repeat this step until $D_{n}^{\prime}$ is no longer a $k$ -dominating set. Suppose that this requires $N$ iterations. Let

$$ \pi=\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\{X_{i,1},X_{i,2}\}\right)\cup\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{N}\{X_{n,1}^{j},X_{n,2}^{j}\}\right). $$

If the remainder of $D_{n}^{\prime}$ does not form a coalition with any set in $\pi$ , then replace $X_{n,1}^{1}$ with $X_{n,1}^{1}\cup D_{n}^{\prime}$ . The union is not a $k$ -dominating set, since this would indicate that $X_{n,1}^{1}$ and $D_{n}^{\prime}$ would have been $k$ -coalition partners. If $D_{n}^{\prime}$ forms a coalition with some set in $\pi$ , we add $D_{n}^{\prime}$ to $\pi$ . Since every $k$ -dominating set is divided into least $2$ sets in this process, we deduce $|\pi|>|\mathcal{D}|$ . We may re-enumerate the sets to obtain that $\pi=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{m}\}$ . ∎

#### Theorem 4.5.

Let $G$ and $H$ be graphs with more than $k$ vertices and let $k\geq 2$ . Then

$$ \COk(G\sqcup H)\leq\COk(G)+\COk(H)-2. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{\COk(G\sqcup H)}\}$ be a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition of $G\sqcup H$ . For simplicity, we will write $S\cap V(G)=\{X\cap V(G)\mid X\in S\text{ and }X\cap V(G)\neq\emptyset\}$ for any subset $S\subseteq\mathfrak{X}$ . By Observation 3.1, no set individually $k$ -dominates both $V(G)$ and $V(H)$ .

(1) If no set $X\in\mathfrak{X}$ individually $k$ -dominates $V(G)$ , then $|\mathfrak{X}|<\COk(H)+\COk(G)$ . The same holds for $V(H)$ .

Note that every set $X\in\mathfrak{X}$ intersects $V(G)$ . Suppose otherwise that there is some set $X$ such that $X\cap V(G)=\emptyset$ . Then $X$ must have a $k$ -coalition partner $X^{\prime}$ such that $X\cup X^{\prime}$ $k$ -dominates $G\sqcup H$ . Therefore, $X^{\prime}$ $k$ -dominates $V(G)$ by itself, a contradiction.

We now show that restricting $\mathfrak{X}$ to $V(G)$ yields a valid $k$ -coalition partition of $V(G)$ . Let $\mathfrak{X}_{G}=\mathfrak{X}\cap V(G)$ . Every set $X\in\mathfrak{X}$ has a $k$ -coalition partner $X^{\prime}$ , where $X\cup X^{\prime}$ is a $k$ -dominating set of $V(G)$ , yet neither $X$ nor $X^{\prime}$ $k$ -dominate $V(G)$ by assumption. Therefore, $\mathfrak{X}_{G}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ with exactly $|\mathfrak{X}|$ sets and $|\mathfrak{X}|=|\mathfrak{X}_{G}|\leq\COk(G)$ . Since $\COk(H)\geq 1$ , we conclude that $|\mathfrak{X}|<\COk(H)+\COk(G)$ . Analogously, if no set in $\mathfrak{X}$ individually $k$ -dominates $V(H)$ , then $|\mathfrak{X}|\leq\COk(H)<\COk(H)+\COk(G)$ . This proves (4).

(2) If $\mathfrak{X}$ contains a set $X_{1}$ that $k$ -dominates $V(G)$ and a set $X_{2}$ that $k$ -dominates $V(H)$ , then $|\mathfrak{X}|<\COk(H)+\COk(G)$ .

By Observation 3.1, there is no $k$ -dominating set of $G\sqcup H$ in $\mathfrak{X}$ , so $X_{1}\neq X_{2}$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle D_{G} \displaystyle=\{X\in\mathfrak{X}\mid X\text{ $k$-dominates }V(G)\}, \displaystyle D_{H} \displaystyle=\{X\in\mathfrak{X}\mid X\text{ $k$-dominates }V(H)\}, \displaystyle P_{G} \displaystyle=\{X\in\mathfrak{X}\setminus(D_{G}\cup D_{H})\mid X\text{ forms a $k$-coalition with some }X^{\prime}\in D_{H}\}, \displaystyle P_{H} \displaystyle=\{X\in\mathfrak{X}\setminus(D_{G}\cup D_{H})\mid X\text{ forms a $k$-coalition with some }X^{\prime}\in D_{G}\}, \displaystyle F \displaystyle=\{X\in\mathfrak{X}\setminus(D_{G}\cup D_{H})\mid X\text{ does not form a $k$-coalition with any }X^{\prime}\in D_{H}\cup D_{G}\}. $$

Note that $\mathfrak{X}=D_{G}\cup D_{H}\cup P_{G}\cup P_{H}\cup F$ , and these subsets are pairwise disjoint with the exception of $P_{G}$ and $P_{H}$ , as there may exist sets that form $k$ -coalitions with sets in both $D_{G}$ and $D_{H}$ .

We first consider the restriction of $\mathfrak{X}$ to $V(G)$ . Observe that $\mathfrak{X}_{G}$ is not necessarily a $k$ -coalition partition of $V(G)$ because some sets in $\mathfrak{X}$ (that do not $k$ -dominate $V(G)$ ) may only form $k$ -coalitions with sets that do $k$ -dominate $V(G)$ . With this in mind, we define

$$ \displaystyle E_{H} \displaystyle=\{X\in D_{H}\mid\text{ every $k$-coalition partner of $X$ is in }D_{G}\}, \displaystyle Q_{H} \displaystyle=\{X\in P_{H}\mid\text{ every $k$-coalition partner of $X$ is in }D_{G}\}. $$

If $X\in E_{H}\cup Q_{H}$ , then $X$ does not $k$ -dominate $V(G)$ but $X$ has no $k$ -coalition partners in $\mathfrak{X}_{G}$ . Since no set in $P_{G}$ or $F$ $k$ -dominates $V(G)$ and each has a $k$ -coalition partner that is not in $D_{G}$ , these sets have a $k$ -coalition partner in $\mathfrak{X}_{G}$ . Therefore, the sets in $E_{H}$ and $Q_{H}$ are precisely the obstructions to $\mathfrak{X}_{G}$ being a $k$ -coalition partition. To address this, our strategy will be as follows: we will merge the vertices of $E_{H}$ and $Q_{H}$ into a single $k$ -dominating set, then use Lemma 4.4 to convert it to a collection of sets, where each has a $k$ -coalition partner in the collection.

By assumption, there exists at least one set $X_{1}\in D_{G}$ . Let

$$ X_{1}^{\prime}=\big(X_{1}\cap V(G)\big)\cup\bigg(\bigcup_{X\in E_{H}}X\cap V(G)\bigg)\cup\bigg(\bigcup_{X\in Q_{H}}X\cap V(G)\bigg). $$

Set $D_{G}^{\prime}=(D_{G}\setminus\{X_{1}\})\cup\{X_{1}^{\prime}\}$ and note that $|D^{\prime}_{G}|=|D_{G}|$ . Define $\overline{D_{H}}=D_{H}\setminus E_{H}$ and $\overline{P_{H}}=P_{H}\backslash Q_{H}$ . Then define

$$ \pi=\Big(D_{G}^{\prime}\cup\overline{D_{H}}\cup\big(P_{G}\setminus(P_{G}\cap P_{H})\big)\cup F\cup\overline{P_{H}}\Big)\cap V(G). $$

Note that we constructed $\pi$ by removing the sets that do not admit a $k$ -coalition partner in $V(G)$ , then reallocating the vertices from these sets to the $k$ -dominating set $X_{1}$ , which we now call $X_{1}^{\prime}$ . Every set $X\in\pi$ that is not a $k$ -dominating set of $V(G)$ has at least one $k$ -coalition partner $X^{\prime}\in\pi$ . The $k$ -dominating sets in $\pi$ are precisely those in $D_{G}^{\prime}\cap V(G)$ . By Lemma 4.4, there is a collection of disjoint sets $D_{G}^{\prime\prime}=\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{d}\}$ , such that every $Y_{i}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with some $Y_{j}$ , $\bigcup_{X\in D^{\prime}_{G}}X=\bigcup_{i=1}^{d}Y_{i}$ , and $|D_{G}^{\prime\prime}|>|D_{G}^{\prime}|$ . Therefore, $\mathfrak{X}_{G}=[D_{G}^{\prime\prime}\cup\overline{D_{H}}\cup P_{G}\cup\overline{P_{H}}\cup F]\cap V(G)$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $V(G)$ and $|\mathfrak{X}_{G}|\leq\COk(G)$ . By analogous reasoning, we get that $\mathfrak{X}_{H}=[D_{H}^{\prime\prime}\cup\overline{D_{G}}\cup P_{H}\cup\overline{P_{G}}\cup F]\cap V(H)$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $V(H)$ and $|\mathfrak{X}_{H}|\leq\COk(H)$ . Combining these, we find that

$$ \displaystyle\COk(G\sqcup H) \displaystyle=|\mathfrak{X}|\leq|D_{G}|+|D_{H}|+|P_{G}|+|P_{H}|+|F| \displaystyle\leq\left(|D_{G}^{\prime\prime}|-1+|\overline{D_{H}}|+|P_{G}|+|\overline{P_{H}}|+|F|\right)+\left(|D_{H}^{\prime\prime}|-1+|\overline{D_{G}}|+|P_{H}|+|\overline{P_{G}}|+|F|\right) \displaystyle=|\mathfrak{X}_{G}|+|\mathfrak{X}_{H}|-2\leq\COk(G)+\COk(H)-2, $$

where the second inequality follows from the fact that $|D_{G}^{\prime\prime}|\geq|D_{G}^{\prime}|+1$ and $|D_{H}^{\prime\prime}|\geq|D_{H}^{\prime}|+1$ . The last equality follows by observing that the collections of sets that compose $\mathfrak{X}_{G}$ (and $\mathfrak{X}_{H}$ ) are disjoint. This proves (4). ∎

We have proven an upper bound on the $k$ -coalition number of the disjoint union of graphs. When the $k$ -coalition partitions of a graph admit a certain “nice” structure, we can also lower-bound the $k$ -coalition number of the disjoint union.

#### Proposition 4.6.

Let $G$ and $H$ be graphs and let $k\geq 2$ . If $G$ admits a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition $\mathfrak{X}_{G}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{\COk(G)}\}$ , where $X_{1}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with every $X_{i}$ for $i>1$ , then

$$ \COk(G\sqcup H)\geq\COk(G). $$

#### Proof.

Let $\mathfrak{X}_{G}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{\COk(G)}\}$ be such a $k$ -coalition partition. Then, by Observation 3.1, $\mathfrak{X}_{G}$ does not contain a $k$ -dominating set of $G$ . Set

$$ \mathfrak{X}_{G\sqcup H}=\{X_{1}\cup V(H)\}\cup\{X_{2},\dots,X_{\COk(G)}\}. $$

Observe that no set in $\mathfrak{X}_{G\sqcup H}$ individually $k$ -dominates $G\sqcup H$ , but every set forms a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}\cup V(H)$ . Then $\mathfrak{X}_{G\sqcup H}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $V(G\sqcup H)$ , and

$$ \COk(G\sqcup H)\geq|\mathfrak{X}_{G}|=\COk(G).\qed $$

By applying Proposition 4.6 to both $G$ and $H$ , we obtain the following result.

#### Corollary 4.7.

Fix $k<\min\{|V(G)|,|V(H)|\}$ . Suppose that $G$ and $H$ admit maximum-size $k$ -coalition partitions $\mathfrak{X}_{G}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{\COk(G)}\}$ and $\mathfrak{X}_{H}=\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{\COk(H)}\}$ , respectively, such that for each $i\in[1,\COk(G)]$ the set $X_{i}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}$ and for each $j\in[1,\COk(H)]$ the set $Y_{j}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with $Y_{1}$ . Then

$$ \COk(G\sqcup H)\geq\max\{\COk(G),\COk(H)\}. $$

While the construction given in the proof of Proposition 4.6 may appear wasteful, the following results demonstrate that the construction is optimal when $k$ is larger than the minimum degrees of $G$ and $H$ .

#### Proposition 4.8.

Fix $k<\min\{|V(G)|,|V(H)|\}$ . If $k>\min\{\delta(G),\delta(H)\}$ , then $\COk(G\sqcup H)\leq\max\{\COk(G),\COk(H)\}$ .

(1) If there is no set in $\mathfrak{X}$ that contains $V^{-}$ , then $|\mathfrak{X}|\leq\max\{\COk(G),\COk(H)\}$ .

The set $X_{1}$ must have a $k$ -coalition partner, say $X_{2}$ , where $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ is a $k$ -dominating set. Then $V^{-}\subseteq X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ and so every other $k$ -dominating set must intersect $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ . Since neither set individually contains $V^{-}$ , it follows that $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ . Since $G$ and $H$ have more than $k$ vertices, each has $k$ -coalition number at least $2$ . The set $X_{i}\cap V(H)$ is either a $k$ -dominating set of $V(H)$ or forms a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}\cap V(H)$ . There are three cases:

(2) If $X_{1}\cap V(H)=\emptyset$ (which may occur when $V^{-}\subseteq V(G)$ ), then $|\mathfrak{X}|\leq\COk(H)$ .

In this setting,

$$ |\mathfrak{X}|=|\mathfrak{X}\cap V(H)|+1. $$

For every $X_{i}\in\mathfrak{X}$ , the set $X_{i}\cap V(H)$ is a $k$ -dominating set of $V(H)$ . Hence, $\mathfrak{X}\cap V(H)$ is a set of $k$ -dominating sets of $V(H)$ . By Lemma 4.4, there is a collection of disjoint sets $\mathfrak{X}_{H}$ such that every set in $\mathfrak{X}_{H}$ has a $k$ -coalition partner in $\mathfrak{X}_{H}$ , $|\mathfrak{X}_{H}|>|\mathfrak{X}|$ , and $\bigcup_{X\in\mathfrak{X}}X\cap V(H)=\bigcup_{Y\in\mathfrak{X}_{H}}Y$ . $$ |\mathfrak{X}\cap V(H)|<|\mathfrak{X}_{H}|\leq\COk(H). $$

Then (4.1) and (4.2) imply that $\COk(G\sqcup H)=|\mathfrak{X}|\leq\COk(H)$ , which proves (4).

If we denote the resulting partition by $\mathfrak{X}_{H}$ , Lemma 4.4 implies that $|\mathfrak{X}|\leq|\mathfrak{X}_{H}|$ . Therefore, $|\mathfrak{X}|=|\mathfrak{X}\cap V(H)|\leq|\mathfrak{X}_{H}|\leq\COk(H)$ , which proves (4).

(4) If $X_{1}\cap V(H)\neq\emptyset$ and, for every $i>1$ , the set $X_{i}\cap V(H)$ is a $k$ -dominating set of $V(H)$ , then $|\mathfrak{X}|\leq\COk(H)$ .

#### Proposition 4.9.

Fix $k<\min\{|V(G)|,|V(H)|\}$ . If $k>\max\{\delta(G),\delta(H)\}$ , then

$$ \COk(G\sqcup H)=\max\{\COk(G),\COk(H)\}. $$

Let $V^{-}_{G}=\{v\in V(G)\mid\deg(v)<k\}$ and $V^{-}_{H}=\{v\in V(H)\mid\deg(v)<k\}$ . By assumption, $V^{-}_{G}\neq\emptyset$ and $V^{-}_{H}\neq\emptyset$ . Set $V^{-}=V^{-}_{G}\cup V^{-}_{H}$ . If $D$ is a $k$ -dominating set of $G\sqcup H$ , then $V^{-}\subseteq D$ .

### When $k$ is large

If $k>\Delta(G\sqcup H)=\max\{\Delta(G),\Delta(H)\}$ , then Observation 3.3 gives

$$ \COk(G\sqcup H)=2=\max\{\COk(G),\COk(H)\}. $$

We now assume that $k\leq\Delta(G\sqcup H)$ .

### Lower bound

Let $\mathfrak{X}_{G}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{\COk(G)}\}$ be a maximum-cardinality $k$ -coalition partition of $V(G)$ . Suppose there exists a set $X_{1}\in\mathfrak{X}_{G}$ such that $V^{-}_{G}\subseteq X_{1}$ . Then for every $i>1$ the set $X_{i}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with only $X_{1}$ . If there is no set $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{G}$ that contains $V^{-}$ , then necessarily $\mathfrak{X}_{G}=\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ where $V^{-}_{G}\subseteq X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ . In this case, it is still true that every set in $\mathfrak{X}\setminus\{X_{1}\}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}$ . By an analogous argument, we can show that for any maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition $\mathfrak{X}_{H}$ of $H$ , there exists a set $Y_{1}$ such that every set in $\mathfrak{X}_{H}\setminus\{Y_{1}\}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with only $Y_{1}$ . By Corollary 4.7, it follows that $\COk(G\sqcup H)\geq\max\{\COk(G),\COk(H)\}$ .

### Upper bound.

Since $k>\max\{\delta(G),\delta(H)\}\geq\min\{\delta(G),\delta(H)\}$ , by Proposition 4.8 we have $\COk(G\sqcup H)\leq\max\{\COk(G),\COk(H)\}$ , as desired. ∎

We may directly apply this proposition to get the following nice corollary.

#### Corollary 4.10.

Let $T_{1},\dots,T_{m}$ be trees with more than $k$ vertices and let $F$ be the forest $F=T_{1}\sqcup T_{2}\sqcup\dots\sqcup T_{m}$ . Then $\COk(F)=\max\{\COk(T_{1}),\COk(T_{2}),\dots,\COk(T_{m})\}$ for all $k\geq 2$ .

We now prove an analogue to Theorem 4.2 for disjoint union.

#### Theorem 4.11.

Fix $k,n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $2\leq k\leq n$ . If $G_{1},\dots,G_{m}$ are (possibly distinct) $n$ -vertex graphs where $m\geq 2$ , then

$$ \COk(G_{1}\sqcup\dots\sqcup G_{m})\leq(n-k+1)(n-k+2)\leq n^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

If $k>\Delta(G_{1}\sqcup\dots\sqcup G_{m})$ , then by Observation 3.3, $\COk(G_{1}\sqcup\dots\sqcup G_{m})=2$ , and since $2\leq k\leq n$ it holds that $2\leq(n-k+1)(n-k+2)$ . We may now assume $k\leq\Delta(G_{1}\sqcup\dots\sqcup G_{m}))$ .

Let $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{\COk(G_{1}\sqcup\dots\sqcup G_{m})}\}$ be a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition of $G_{1}\sqcup\dots\sqcup G_{m}$ . Each $X_{i}\in\mathfrak{X}$ intersects $G_{1}$ or forms a coalition with some set $X_{j}$ that intersects $G_{1}$ . By Observation 3.1, there are no $k$ -dominating sets in $\mathfrak{X}$ . Therefore, there exist two $k$ -coalition partners $X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathfrak{X}$ whose union $k$ -dominates $G_{1}$ and $|(X_{1}\cup X_{2})\cap G_{1}|\geq k$ . There are at most $n-k+2$ sets in $\mathfrak{X}\setminus\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ that intersect $G_{1}$ . By Lemma 3.4, each such set has at most $\Delta(G_{1}\sqcup\dots\sqcup G_{m})-k+3\leq(n-1)-k+2$ distinct $k$ -coalition partners. Then

$$ \COk(G_{1}\sqcup\dots\sqcup G_{m})=|\mathfrak{X}|\leq(n-k+1)(n-k+2)\leq n^{2}, $$

where the last inequality follows from the fact that $k\geq 2$ . ∎

#### Corollary 4.12.

Fix $k,n,m\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $2\leq k\leq n$ and $2\leq m$ . For any $n$ -vertex graph $G$ ,

$$ \COk(m*G)\leq n^{2}, $$

where $m*G=G\sqcup\dots\sqcup G$ denotes the disjoint union of a graph with itself $m$ times.

## 5. Distinct sizes of $k$ -coalition partitions

The previous work on $k$ -coalitions by Jafari, Alikhani, and Bakhshesh [15] and Brešar, Henning, and Samadi [6] has focused on computing and bounding the $k$ -coalition number. Haynes, Hedetniemi, Hedetniemi, McRae, and Mohan [8] proposed the study of the minimum number of sets in a coalition partition. This was investigated by Bakhshesh and Henning [4]. In this section, we generalize this to the minimum $k$ -coalition number, which we denote by $\cok(G)$ . We also propose a new question: what are all possible sizes of the $k$ -coalition partitions of a given graph? To this end, we provide some definitions.

#### Definition 5.1.

Let $\cok(G)$ denote the minimum number of sets in any $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ . Let

$$ \text{I}_{k}(G)=\{n\in\mathbb{N}\mid\text{there exists a $k$-coalition partition of $G$ with exactly $n$ sets}\}. $$

By definition, $\text{I}_{k}(G)\subseteq[\cok(G),\COk(G)]$ ; the main theorem of this section will show that $\text{I}_{k}(G)$ is the entire interval.

#### Theorem 5.2.

Fix $k\geq 2$ . Let $G$ be a graph. The set $\text{I}_{k}(G)$ is the interval $\left[\cok(G),\COk(G)\right]$ .

The proof is divided into cases depending on the relationships between $k$ and $\delta(G)$ . We first prove a few results that we will require later.

#### Proposition 5.3.

Let $k\leq n$ . The minimum $k$ -coalition partition number of $K_{n}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\cok(K_{n})=\begin{cases}\frac{n}{k}&\text{if $k\mid n$},\\
\lceil\frac{n}{k}\rceil&\text{if $k\nmid n$ and $k\nmid n+1$},\\
\lceil\frac{n}{k}\rceil+1&\text{if $k\nmid n$ and $k\mid n+1$}.\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

Let $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{\cok(G)}\}$ be a minimum-size $k$ -coalition partition of $K_{n}$ . Label the vertices of $K_{n}$ as $\{v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\}$ . For every $X_{i}\in\mathfrak{X}$ , we have $|X_{i}|\leq k$ as otherwise $X_{i}$ would be a $k$ -dominating set with strictly greater than $k$ vertices. By the pigeonhole principle, $|\mathfrak{X}|\geq\lceil\frac{n}{k}\rceil$ . There are three cases:

(1) If $k\mid n$ , then $\cok(K_{n})=\frac{n}{k}$ .

If $k\mid n$ , then $|\mathfrak{X}|\geq\frac{n}{k}$ . We obtain the upper bound from the $k$ -coalition partition consisting of $\frac{n}{k}$ disjoint $k$ -dominating sets, each with exactly $k$ vertices. This proves (5).

(2) If $k\nmid n$ and $k\nmid n+1$ , then $\cok(K_{n})=\left\lceil\frac{n}{k}\right\rceil$ .

Since we showed $\cok(K_{n})\geq\left\lceil\frac{n}{k}\right\rceil$ , it suffices to exhibit a $k$ -coalition partition with exactly $\left\lceil\frac{n}{k}\right\rceil$ sets. Let $m=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{k}\right\rfloor$ and let $D_{i}=\{v_{ik+1},\dots,v_{(i+1)k}\}$ . Then $D_{i}$ is a $k$ -dominating set with exactly $k$ vertices and the following is a $k$ -coalition partition:

$$ \mathfrak{X}=\left\{D_{0},\dots,D_{m-2}\right\}\cup\left\{\{v_{(m-1)k+1},\dots,v_{mk-1}\}\right\}\cup\left\{\{v_{mk},\dots,v_{n}\}\right\}. $$

Since $k\nmid n+1$ , it must be that $mk<n<(m+1)k-1$ . Therefore, the latter two sets both have strictly fewer than $k$ vertices, while their union has at least $k$ vertices, and so these two sets form a $k$ -coalition. This proves (5).

(3) If $k\nmid n$ and $k\mid n+1$ , then $\cok(K_{n})=\left\lceil\frac{n}{k}\right\rceil+1$ .

In this case, the partition in (5.1) is not a $k$ -coalition partition because $k\mid n+1$ implies that $n=(m+1)k-1$ , and so the set $\left\{v_{mk},\dots,v_{n}\right\}$ is a $k$ -dominating set with $k$ vertices. Consequently, the set $\left\{v_{(m-1)k+1},\dots,v_{mk-1}\right\}$ does not have a $k$ -coalition partner. In fact, every partition of $V(K_{n})$ into $\left\lceil\frac{n}{k}\right\rceil$ sets (where each set has no more than $k$ vertices) has exactly one set with $k-1$ vertices and no $k$ -coalition partner. Consequently, $\cok(G)>\left\lceil\frac{n}{k}\right\rceil$ . However, if we define $D_{i}$ as above and set

$$ \mathfrak{X}=\left\{D_{0},\dots,D_{m-2}\right\}\cup\left\{\{v_{(m-1)k+1},\dots,v_{mk-1}\}\right\}\cup\left\{\{v_{mk},\dots,v_{n-1}\}\right\}\cup\{v_{n}\}, $$

then $\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ into $\left\lceil\frac{n}{k}\right\rceil+1$ sets, which proves (5). See Figure 4 for an example of this construction. ∎

The only case where a $k$ -coalition partition can consist of exactly one set occurs when the graph $G$ has exactly $k$ vertices. The following lemma handles this edge case.

#### Lemma 5.4.

If $|V(G)|=k\geq 2$ , then $\text{I}_{k}(G)=[1,2]$ .

#### Proof.

If $|V(G)|=k$ , then $\Delta(G)<k$ . By Observation 3.3 $\COk(G)=2$ and, in particular, there exists a $k$ -coalition partition with two sets. In addition, $\{V(G)\}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition with one set. ∎

The following results address the three cases: $k>\delta(G)$ , $k=\delta(G)$ , and $k<\delta(G)$ . When $k>\delta(G)$ , there exists at least one vertex $v$ with degree less than $k$ and every $k$ -dominating set of $G$ must contain $v$ .

#### Lemma 5.5.

Fix $k\geq 2$ . If $k>\delta(G)$ and $|V(G)|\neq k$ , then $\text{I}_{k}(G)=[2,\COk(G)]$ .

#### Proof.

The strategy is to fix a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition and then carefully merge sets such that the resulting partition is still a $k$ -coalition partition. Let $V^{-}=\{v\in V\mid\deg(v)<k\}$ . Let $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{\COk(G)}\}$ be a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition. Suppose there does not exist a set $X\in\mathfrak{X}$ such that $V^{-}\subseteq X$ . Then $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ , where $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ are $k$ -coalition partners and $V^{-}\subseteq X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ . In this case, $\COk(G)=2$ .

We may now assume there exists some set $X\in\mathfrak{X}$ such that $V^{-}\subseteq X$ ; without loss of generality, say $V^{-}\subseteq X_{1}$ . For every $i>1$ , the set $X_{i}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set (since it does not contain $V^{-}$ ). Moreover, $X_{i}$ can form a $k$ -coalition with only $X_{1}$ . So, for every $n\in[2,\COk(G)]$ , let

$$ \mathfrak{X}_{n}=\left\{X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n-1},X_{n}\cup\dots\cup X_{\COk(G)}\right\}. $$

For every $n\geq 2$ , the set $X_{n}\cup\dots\cup X_{\COk(G)}$ is not $k$ -dominating (since it does not contain $V^{-}$ ) and forms a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}$ . Hence, $\mathfrak{X}_{n}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ with exactly $n$ sets. ∎

We next consider the case where $k=\delta(G)$ . If $v$ is a vertex of minimum degree, we observe that every $k$ -dominating set contains either $v$ or the entire neighborhood of $v$ .

#### Lemma 5.6.

Let $k=\delta(G)$ and $k\geq 2$ . If $k=2$ and $G=K_{3}$ , then $\text{I}_{k}(G)=\{3\}$ . Otherwise, $\text{I}_{k}(G)=[2,\COk(G)]$ .

#### Proof.

Let $v\in V(G)$ be a vertex of minimum degree. If every vertex $u\in V(G)\setminus\{v\}$ is adjacent to $v$ , then $|V(G)|=k+1$ and every vertex has degree $k$ . Therefore, $G$ is the clique $K_{k+1}$ . By Lemma 3.2, $\COk(K_{k+1})=(k+1)-k+2=3$ . If $k=2$ , then $G=K_{3}$ . There is no $2$ -coalition partition of $K_{3}$ with two sets, since if we partition $V(K_{3})$ into two sets, then one set contains one vertex, say $X_{1}$ , and one set contains two vertices, say $X_{2}$ . However, $X_{1}$ has no $2$ -coalition partner because $X_{2}$ is a $2$ -dominating set with $2$ vertices. Therefore, the only $2$ -coalition partition of $K_{3}$ is the partition into three singleton sets, and so $I_{2}(K_{3})=\{3\}$ . If $k>2$ , then $k\nmid(k+1)+1$ . By Proposition 5.3, $\cok(K_{k+1})=\left\lceil\frac{k+1}{k}\right\rceil=2$ . We conclude that $\text{I}_{k}(K_{k+1})=[2,3]$ for all $k\geq 3$ .

We may now assume that $V(G)\setminus N[v]\neq\emptyset$ . We first construct a $k$ -coalition partition with two sets. Pick some $u\in N(v)$ and set $\mathfrak{X}=\{V(G)\setminus\{v,u\},\{v,u\}\}$ . The set $V(G)\setminus\{v,u\}$ does not $k$ -dominate $v$ because it neither contains $v$ nor the entire neighborhood of $v$ . The set $\{v,u\}$ does not $k$ -dominate the vertices in $V(G)\setminus N[v]$ since $k\geq 2$ . However, the union of these sets $k$ -dominates $G$ . Therefore, $\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition.

It just remains to construct $k$ -coalition partitions with $n$ sets, where $n\in[3,\COk(G)]$ and $\COk(G)\geq 3$ . Fix a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition $\mathfrak{X}$ of $G$ and define

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{1}=\{X\in\mathfrak{X}\mid X\cap N[v]\neq\emptyset\}; \displaystyle\pi_{2}=\{X\in\mathfrak{X}\mid X\cap N[v]=\emptyset\}. $$

Set $p_{1}=|\pi_{1}|$ and $p_{2}=|\pi_{2}|$ ; it may be that $\pi_{2}=\emptyset$ . Then $\COk(G)=p_{1}+p_{2}$ . Label the sets in $\pi_{1}$ as $X_{1},\dots,X_{p_{1}}$ and the sets in $\pi_{2}$ as $Y_{1},\dots,Y_{p_{2}}$ , such that $X_{1}$ is the set containing $v$ .

For each $n\in[3,p_{1}]$ , we will construct a $k$ -coalition partition with $n$ sets. First suppose $p_{1}\geq 3$ . Then $X_{2}$ must contain some neighbor of $v$ but not all of $N(v)$ . Let $Y=Y_{1}\cup Y_{2}\cup\dots\cup Y_{p_{2}}$ . Note that if $\pi_{2}=\emptyset$ , then $Y=\emptyset$ . We verify that the following is a $k$ -coalition partition with $n$ sets:

$$ \{X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n-1}\}\cup\{X_{n}\cup\dots\cup X_{p_{1}}\cup Y\}. $$

Indeed, the set $X_{n}\cup\dots\cup X_{p_{1}}\cup Y$ is not a $k$ -dominating set because it contains at most $k-1$ neighbors of $v$ and does not $k$ -dominate $v$ . Since the union of $X_{p_{1}}$ with any of the sets $X_{3},\dots,X_{p_{1}-1},Y$ does not form a $k$ -dominating set (since it cannot $k$ -dominate $v$ ), the $k$ -coalition partner of $X_{p_{1}}$ in the initial partition must have been $X_{1}$ or $X_{2}$ . Therefore, $X_{n}\cup\dots\cup X_{p_{1}}\cup Y$ forms a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}$ or $X_{2}$ .

If $p_{2}=0$ , we are done because $p_{1}=\COk(G)$ , where we assumed $\COk(G)\geq 3$ . Suppose $\pi_{2}\neq\emptyset$ . Then, for every $n\in[p_{1}+1,\COk(G)]$ , the following is a $k$ -coalition partition with $n$ sets:

$$ \pi_{1}\cup\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n-p_{1}-1}\}\cup\{Y_{n-p_{1}}\cup\dots\cup Y_{p_{2}}\}. $$

Indeed, the set $Y_{n-p_{1}}\cup\dots\cup Y_{p_{2}}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set because it does not $k$ -dominate $v$ (since it contains no neighbors of $v$ ). However, this set forms a $k$ -coalition with the $k$ -coalition partner(s) of $Y_{n-p_{1}},\dots,Y_{p_{2}}$ in $\pi_{1}$ . Note that this construction shows that if $p_{1}=1$ then $[2,\COk(G)]\subseteq\text{I}_{k}(G)$ and if $p_{1}=2$ then $[3,\COk(G)]\subseteq\text{I}_{k}(G)$ , as required. ∎

The $k<\delta(G)$ case is the hardest and the proof requires two approaches. First, we begin with a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ and strategically merge sets one-by-one to gradually decrease the number of sets, as we did in the previous proof. Second, we start with a minimum-size $k$ -coalition partition, then carefully rearrange the sets and split off singletons one-by-one to gradually increase the number of sets.

#### Lemma 5.7.

Fix $k\geq 2$ . If $k<\delta(G)$ , then $[\delta(G)-k+4,\COk(G)]\subseteq\text{I}_{k}(G)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathfrak{X}$ be a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ and let $v$ be a vertex of minimum degree. By Observation 3.1, $\mathfrak{X}$ does not contain any $k$ -dominating sets. Define

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{1}=\{X\in\mathfrak{X}\mid X\cap N[v]\neq\emptyset\}; \displaystyle\pi_{2}=\{X\in\mathfrak{X}\mid X\cap N[v]=\emptyset\}. $$

As before, let $p_{1}=|\pi_{1}|$ and $p_{2}=|\pi_{2}|$ . Label the sets of $\pi_{1}$ and $\pi_{2}$ as $X_{1},\dots,X_{p_{1}}$ and $Y_{1},\dots,Y_{p_{2}}$ , respectively. When $\pi_{2}\neq\emptyset$ , for every $n\in[p_{1}+1,\COk(G)]$ , the following is a $k$ -coalition partition with $n$ sets:

$$ \pi_{1}\cup\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n-p_{1}-1}\}\cup\{Y_{n-p_{1}}\cup\dots\cup Y_{p_{2}}\}. $$

Let $Y=Y_{1}\cup\dots\cup Y_{p_{2}}$ . Let $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime}=\{X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{p_{1}}\}\cup\{Y\}$ . Note that $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime}$ does not contain a $k$ -dominating set, since $\mathfrak{X}$ did not contain a $k$ -dominating set and the new set $Y$ does not $k$ -dominate $v$ . If there exist $X,X^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{X}^{\prime}$ that are not $k$ -coalition partners, then replace $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime}$ with $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime\prime}=(\mathfrak{X}^{\prime}\setminus\{X,X^{\prime}\})\cup\{X\cup X^{\prime}\}$ . We call this merging two sets. Observe that $X\cup X^{\prime}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set (otherwise, $X$ and $X^{\prime}$ would have been $k$ -coalition partners), but $X\cup X^{\prime}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with the $k$ -coalition partners of $X$ and $X^{\prime}$ . And, if some set $X^{\prime\prime}$ formed a coalition with $X$ or $X^{\prime}$ , it now forms a coalition with $X\cup X^{\prime}$ . Therefore, we conclude that $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime\prime}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition, with one fewer set than $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime}$ . Repeat until no suitable $X$ and $X^{\prime}$ remain.

Let $\mathfrak{X}^{\star}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{r},Y\}$ be the resulting $k$ -coalition partition. Through the merging process, we have constructed a $k$ -coalition partition with $n$ sets for every $|\mathfrak{X}^{\star}|<n<|\mathfrak{X}^{\prime}|$ . Let $X_{1}$ denote the set containing $v$ and let $Y$ denote the set that does not intersect $N[v]$ , if such a set exists.

(1) It holds that $|\mathfrak{X}^{\star}|\leq\left\lceil\frac{2\delta(G)}{k}\right\rceil+2$ .

Let $\pi_{3}=\mathfrak{X}^{\star}\setminus\{X_{1},Y\}$ , then every set in $\pi_{3}$ intersects $N(v)$ . Set $|\pi_{3}|=p_{3}$ . If there exist two sets $X,X^{\prime}\in\pi_{3}$ that both contain fewer than $\frac{k}{2}$ neighbors of $v$ , then their union $X\cup X^{\prime}$ does not $k$ -dominate $v$ . Hence, $X$ and $X^{\prime}$ are not $k$ -coalition partners and could be merged. However, since the merging process has terminated, there is at most one set $X\in\pi_{3}$ with $|N(v)\cap X|<\frac{k}{2}$ .

Suppose, for contradiction, $|\mathfrak{X}^{\star}|\geq\left\lceil\frac{2\delta(G)}{k}\right\rceil+3$ , then $p_{3}\geq\left\lceil\frac{2\delta(G)}{k}\right\rceil+1.$ If $k=2$ , then $p_{3}>\delta(G)$ , which contradicts the fact that every set in $\pi_{3}$ intersects $N(v)$ . We may now assume $k\geq 3$ . All but one set, say $X\in\pi_{3}$ , contain at least $\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}\right\rceil$ neighbors of $v$ . Note that $X$ has nonzero intersection with $N[v]$ , so it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\delta(G)\geq\left\lceil\frac{2\delta(G)}{k}\right\rceil\cdot\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}\right\rceil+|X\cap N(v)|\geq\delta(G)+|X\cap N(v)|>\delta(G). $$

This is a contradiction, which proves (5).

We have now constructed a $k$ -coalition partition with at most $\left\lceil\frac{2\delta(G)}{k}\right\rceil+2$ sets. It is sufficient to observe that for all $2\leq k<\delta(G)$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\lceil\frac{2\delta(G)}{k}\right\rceil+2=\left\lceil 2+\frac{2}{k}\cdot(\delta(G)-k)\right\rceil+2\leq\big\lceil 2+\delta(G)-k\big\rceil+2=\delta(G)-k+4, $$

concluding the proof. ∎

#### Lemma 5.8.

Fix $k\geq 2$ . If $k<\delta(G)$ , then $[\cok(G),\delta(G)-k+3]\subseteq\text{I}_{k}(G)$ .

#### Proof.

Fix a minimum size $k$ -coalition partition $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{\cok(G)}\}$ . If every set in $\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -dominating set, then split $X_{1}$ into two non-empty sets $X_{1}$ and $X_{\cok(G)+1}$ that form a $k$ -coalition pair. We now may suppose that at least one set in $\mathfrak{X}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set; without loss of generality, $X_{1}$ is such a set. Let $m$ be the number of sets in the smallest $k$ -coalition partition with at least one $k$ -coalition pair. By definition, $\cok(G)\leq m\leq\cok(G)+1$ .

If there exists a vertex $u\in X_{i}$ , for some $i\neq 1$ , such that $\{u\}\cup X_{1}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set, then replace $X_{1}$ by $X_{1}\cup\{u\}$ and replace $X_{i}$ by $X_{i}\setminus\{u\}$ . Denote the new $k$ -coalition partition by $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime}$ . Repeat this step with $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime}$ until no such vertex can be found. Let $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime\prime}$ be the resulting partition.

(1) The collection $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime\prime}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ with at most $m$ sets.

At every step in the process, the number of sets in the partition either stays the same or decreases, hence $|\mathfrak{X}^{\prime\prime}|\leq|\mathfrak{X}|=m$ . With the exception of $X_{1}$ , no other set gains vertices. Therefore, if a set was not previously a $k$ -dominating set with $k$ vertices, it did not become one. Second, when the process terminates, the set $\{u\}\cup X_{1}$ is a $k$ -dominating set for every $u\in V(G)\setminus X_{1}$ . Therefore, for each $X_{i}$ where $i\neq 1$ , one of the following holds: either $X_{i}$ is a $k$ -dominating set with exactly $k$ vertices or $X_{i}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}$ . This proves (5).

Given that $X_{1}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set, there exists at least one vertex, say $v\in V(G)\setminus X_{1}$ , that is not $k$ -dominated by $X_{1}$ . We make two structural observations.

(2) If $v\in V(G)\setminus X_{1}$ is not $k$ -dominated by $X_{1}$ , then $|N(v)\cap X_{1}|=k-1$ and $V(G)\setminus N[v]\subseteq X_{1}$ .

Since $X_{1}$ does not $k$ -dominate $v$ , it must be that $|N(v)\cap X_{1}|\leq k-1$ . However, if $X_{1}$ has strictly fewer than $k-1$ neighbors of $v$ , then for any $v^{\prime}\in N(v)\cap(V(G)\setminus X_{1})$ , the set $\{v^{\prime}\}\cup X_{1}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set, contradicting the assumption that the process terminated. This proves the first claim.

To prove the second claim, assume otherwise that there exists some vertex $u\notin X_{1}$ and $u\in V(G)\setminus N[v]$ . Then $\{u\}\cup X_{1}$ would not $k$ -dominate $v$ , contradicting the assumption that the process had terminated. This proves (5).

Now, we have the $k$ -coalition partition $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime\prime}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{m}\}$ , where $X_{i}\subseteq N[v]$ for all $i\geq 2$ . We define a splitting process analogously to the merging process. If there is a set $X\in\mathfrak{X}^{\prime\prime}\setminus\{X_{1}\}$ where $|X|\geq 2$ , then split $X$ into two sets: a singleton set $\{u\}$ and $X\setminus\{u\}$ . Set $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime\prime\prime}=\big(\mathfrak{X}^{\prime\prime}\setminus\{X\}\big)\cup\{u\}\cup X\setminus\{u\}$ .

We verify that $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime\prime}$ is a $k$ -coalition after the splitting step. Since every vertex in $X$ forms a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}$ , clearly both $\{u\}$ and $X\setminus\{u\}$ form a $k$ -coalition with $X$ . Even if $X$ is a $k$ -dominating set with $k$ -vertices, the set $X\setminus\{u\}$ has fewer than $k$ vertices and cannot $k$ -dominate $G$ . Repeat the splitting step until every set in the partition, except $X_{1}$ , is a singleton set. Let $\mathfrak{X}^{\star}$ denote the resulting partition. The number of sets in $\mathfrak{X}^{\star}$ is at least

$$ |\mathfrak{X}^{\star}|=(\deg(v)+1)-(k-1)+1\geq\delta(G)-k+3. $$

In the course of this splitting process, we obtain $k$ -coalition partitions of all intermediate sizes between $\cok(G)$ and $|\mathfrak{X}^{\prime\prime}|$ . We conclude that $[\cok(G),\delta(G)-k+3]\subseteq\text{I}_{k}(G)$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 5.2.

Fix $k\geq 2$ . If the graph $G$ has exactly $k$ vertices, then by Lemma 5.4 $\text{I}_{k}(G)=[1,2]$ . Otherwise, $\cok(G)\geq 2$ . If $k\geq\delta(G)$ , then by Lemma 5.5 and Lemma 5.6, there are only two cases.

- (1) If $k=2$ and $G=K_{3}$ , then $I_{2}(K_{3})=\{3\}$ .

- (2) Otherwise, $\text{I}_{k}(G)=[2,\COk(G)]$ .

In either case, we have $\text{I}_{k}(G)=[\cok(G),\COk(G)]$ . If $k<\delta(G)$ , then by Lemma 5.7 and Lemma 5.8, it follows that $[\delta(G)-k+4,\COk(G)]\subseteq\text{I}_{k}(G)$ and $[\cok(G),\delta(G)-k+3]\subseteq\text{I}_{k}(G)$ . Therefore, $\text{I}_{k}(G)=[\cok(G),\COk(G)]$ . ∎

We conclude by providing necessary and sufficient conditions on $G$ to obtain that $\cok(G)=2$ .

#### Theorem 5.9.

Fix $k\geq 2$ . Suppose $G$ is a non-complete graph with more than $k$ vertices. Then $\cok(G)=2$ if and only if there exist two vertices $u$ and $v$ such that $|N[u]\cap N[v]|\leq 2k-2$ .

#### Proof.

First, suppose that there exists a $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ with two sets, say $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ . We will find two vertices $u$ and $v$ with $|N[u]\cap N[v]|\leq 2k-2$ . We consider two cases: Case 1: If $X_{1}$ is a $k$ -dominating set with $k$ vertices, then $X_{2}$ is also a $k$ -dominating set with $k$ vertices. So $|V(G)|=|X_{1}|+|X_{2}|=2k$ . Given that $G$ is not a complete graph, there exist at least two nonadjacent vertices $v$ and $u$ . Since $u,v\notin N[u]\cap N[v]$ , we have $|N[u]\cap N[v]|\leq 2k-2$ .

Case 2: Suppose that $X_{1}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set. Then $X_{2}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set. Therefore, there is at least one vertex $v\in X_{2}$ that is not $k$ -dominated by $X_{1}$ and at least one vertex $u\in X_{1}$ that is not $k$ -dominated by $X_{2}$ . This implies

$$ |N[v]\cap X_{1}|\leq k-1\text{ and }|N[u]\cap X_{2}|\leq k-1. $$

Then it follows that

$$ \big|N[u]\cap N[v]\big|=\big|N[u]\cap N[v]\cap X_{1}\big|+\big|N[u]\cap N[v]\cap X_{2}\big|\leq 2k-2. $$

Now, to prove the rest of the statement, assume that there exist two vertices $u$ and $v$ such that $|N[u]\cap N[v]|\leq 2k-2$ . We will construct a $k$ -coalition partition with exactly two sets.

First suppose $\min(\deg(u),\deg(v))\leq k-2$ ; without loss of generality $\deg(v)\leq k-2$ . Then $\{N[v],G\setminus N[v]\}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ . Indeed, $G\setminus N[v]$ cannot $k$ -dominate $v$ and, since $|N[v]|\leq k-1$ , does not $k$ -dominate any vertex in $G\setminus N[v]$ (which is non-empty because $|V(G)|\geq k$ ). We may now assume both $\deg(u),\deg(v)\geq k-1$ . Let $\deg(v)=d$ and label the vertices of $N(v)$ as $\{v_{1},\dots,v_{d}\}$ . If $u$ and $v$ are adjacent, relabel such that $v_{1}=u$ . If $|N[u]\cap N(v)|\leq k-1$ , suppose that $N[u]\cap N(v)\subseteq\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k-1}\}$ . Otherwise, let $\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k-1}\}\subseteq N(v)\cap N[u]$ . Let

$$ \displaystyle X_{1}=\left(V(G)\setminus N[v]\right)\cup\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k-1}\}; \displaystyle X_{2}=\{v,v_{k},v_{k+1},\dots,v_{d}\}. $$

Observe that $v\in X_{2}$ is not $k$ -dominated by $X_{1}$ , which contains at most $k-1$ neighbors of $v$ and $u\in X_{1}$ is not $k$ -dominated by $X_{2}$ which contains at most $k-1$ neighbors of $u$ . Therefore, $\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition. ∎

#### Corollary 5.10.

Fix $k\geq 2$ . If $k<\delta(G)$ , then any one of the following conditions is sufficient to ensure that $G$ has $\cok(G)=2$ .

- (1) $G$ is not connected;

- (2) $\operatorname{diam}(G)\geq 3;$

- (3) $\delta(G)\leq 2k-2.$

## 6. $k$ -coalition graphs

In this section, we study $k$ -coalition graphs as proposed by Jafari, Alikhani, and Bakhshesh [15], which generalize the coalition graphs initially proposed in [8] and further studied in [11, 10, 12]. We provide a structural characterization of the $k$ -coalition graph when $k\leq\delta(G)$ and we show that every graph admits a $k$ -coalition partition such that the resulting $k$ -coalition graph is a complete graph. The main theorem of this section establishes that every graph is the $k$ -coalition graph of some other graph. The result was shown for $k=1$ by Haynes, Hedetniemi, Hedetniemi, McRae, and Mohan in [11]. Their proof proceeds by explicit construction, and we generalize it for all $k$ .

#### Definition 6.1.

Let $G$ be a graph. Let $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{|\mathfrak{X}|}\}$ be a $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ . The $k$ -coalition graph, denoted by $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ , is the graph with vertex set $\{x_{1},\dots,x_{|\mathfrak{X}|}\}$ , where two vertices $x_{i}$ and $x_{j}$ are adjacent if and only if $X_{i}$ and $X_{j}$ form a $k$ -coalition. By definition, if $X_{i}\in\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -dominating set, then $x_{i}$ is an isolated vertex in $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ . See Figure 5 for an example.

#### Proposition 6.2.

Let $G$ be a graph and fix $k>\delta(G)$ . If $\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ with $n$ sets, then $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ is the star $S_{n-1}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{n}\}$ be a $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ and let $V^{-}=\{v\in V(G)\mid\deg(v)<k\}$ . If $D$ is a $k$ -dominating set of $G$ , then $V^{-}\subseteq D$ . Suppose that there is no set $X$ in $\mathfrak{X}$ such that $V^{-}\subseteq X$ . Then $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ , where $V^{-}\subseteq X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ . Since $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ are $k$ -coalition partners, $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)=S_{1}$ . We may now suppose that (relabeling if necessary) $V^{-}\subseteq X_{1}$ . Then, for every $i>1$ , the set $X_{i}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}$ and does not form a $k$ -coalition with any set $X_{j}$ where $j\neq 1$ . Suppose $x_{i}$ is the vertex in $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ corresponding to the set $X_{i}$ . Then two vertices $x_{i}$ and $x_{j}$ with $i<j$ are adjacent if and only if $i=1$ . Thus, $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)=S_{n-1}$ . ∎

#### Definition 6.3.

A modified bistar is a graph with vertex set $\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{|V(G)|}\}$ where $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ are centers and every vertex $v_{i}$ , for $i\geq 3$ , is adjacent to $v_{1}$ , $v_{2}$ , or both. Moreover, $v_{i}$ is not adjacent to $v_{j}$ for any $j\geq 3$ . This graph is not necessarily connected. See Figure 6 for an example.

#### Proposition 6.4.

Suppose $k=\delta(G)$ and $\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ with $n\geq 2$ sets. Then the $k$ -coalition graph $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ has one of the following two structures:

- (1) Star $S_{n-1}$ ;

- (2) Modified bistar.

#### Proof.

Let $\mathfrak{X}$ be a $k$ -coalition partition with sets $X_{1},\dots,X_{n}$ and let $x_{i}$ be the vertex in $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ corresponding to $X_{i}$ . Let $v\in V(G)$ be a vertex of minimum degree. Relabeling if necessary, suppose that $v\in X_{1}$ . Since $v$ has degree $k$ , any $k$ -dominating set must either contain $v$ or contain the entire neighborhood $N(v)$ .

(1) If $X_{1}$ is a $k$ -dominating set with exactly $k$ vertices, then $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ is a modified bistar.

Since $|V(G)|\geq|N[v]|=k+1>|X_{1}|$ , there are is at least one other set in $\mathfrak{X}$ . Since the union of the remaining sets must $k$ -dominate $v$ (without containing $v$ ), we have $N(v)\cap X_{1}=\emptyset$ . Relabeling if necessary, suppose that $X_{2}$ intersects $N(v)$ . If $X_{2}$ is a $k$ -dominating set, then there are no other sets in $\mathfrak{X}$ since the remaining sets could not $k$ -dominate $v$ . In this case, $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ and $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ is the star $S_{1}$ . If $X_{2}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set, then every set $X$ in $\mathfrak{X}\setminus\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ can only form a $k$ -coalition with $X_{2}$ . Therefore, in $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ , every vertex $x_{i}$ for $i\geq 3$ is adjacent only to $x_{2}$ while $x_{1}$ is a singleton. This proves (6).

(2) If $X_{1}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set, then $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ is a modified bistar.

First, suppose that for each $i\geq 2$ the set $X_{i}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with only $X_{1}$ . Then every vertex $x_{i}$ in $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ is only adjacent to $x_{1}$ . Therefore, $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ is the star $S_{n-1}$ .

Now, suppose that there exists at least one set that does not form a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}$ . Then, there must be a set $X_{2}$ that intersects $N(v)$ . This implies that every set $X_{i}\in\mathfrak{X}$ for $i\geq 3$ must form a $k$ -coalition with $X_{1}$ (then the union contains $v$ ) or $X_{2}$ (then the union contains the entire neighborhood of $v$ ). For any $i,j\geq 3$ , the sets $X_{i}$ and $X_{j}$ do not form a $k$ -coalition because $X_{i}\cup X_{j}$ does not $k$ -dominate $v$ . If $X_{2}$ is a $k$ -dominating set, then every other set must form a $k$ -coalition with only $X_{1}$ . Therefore, in $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ , every vertex $x_{i}$ for $i\geq 3$ is adjacent to $x_{1}$ or $x_{2}$ , and not adjacent to any $x_{j}$ with $j\geq 3$ . We conclude that $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ is a modified bistar. ∎

#### Proposition 6.5.

Every graph $G$ has some $k$ -coalition partition $\mathfrak{X}$ such that $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)$ is a complete graph.

#### Proof.

Let $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{n}\}$ be a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ . By Observation 3.1, there are no $k$ -dominating sets in $\mathfrak{X}$ . We now perform a merging process. If there exist two sets $X,X^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{X}$ that are not $k$ -coalition partners, let $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime}=(\mathfrak{X}\setminus\{X,X^{\prime}\})\cup\{X\cup X^{\prime}\}$ . Since neither $X$ nor $X^{\prime}$ individually $k$ -dominates $G$ , and they do not form a $k$ -coalition, it follows that $X\cup X^{\prime}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set. Thus, $\mathfrak{X}^{\prime}$ contains no $k$ -dominating sets. In fact, $\mathfrak{X}$ is still a $k$ -coalition partition because any set that previously formed a $k$ -coalition with $X$ or $X^{\prime}$ will now form a $k$ -coalition with $X\cup X^{\prime}$ . Repeat the merging step until all pairs of sets in the partition are $k$ -coalition partners. Let $\pi=\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{m}\}$ denote the resulting partition. Since every two sets $Y_{i}$ and $Y_{j}$ form a $k$ -coalition, every two vertices $y_{i}$ and $y_{j}$ in $\operatorname{kCG}(\pi,G)$ are adjacent, as required. ∎

#### Theorem 6.6.

For every graph $H$ and every $k\geq 2$ , there exists a graph $G$ and some $k$ -coalition partition $\mathfrak{X}$ of $G$ , such that $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)=H$ .

#### Proof.

The proof follows by explicit construction. See Figure 5 for an example. The $k=1$ case is handled in [11] and we generalize the construction to any $k\geq 2$ . Write $V(H)=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\}\cup\{u_{1},\dots,u_{m}\}$ , where every vertex $v_{i}$ has degree at least $1$ and every $u_{i}$ is an isolated vertex. Let $H^{\prime}$ be the subgraph induced by $V(H)\setminus\{u_{1},\dots,u_{m}\}$ . Note that $E(H^{\prime})=E(H)$ .

We begin the construction of $G$ with the complete $n$ -partite graph, where every partite set has $k$ vertices. The vertex set is initially $V(K_{k,\dots,k})=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\{x_{i,1},x_{i,2},\dots,x_{i,k}\}$ , where $x_{i,j}$ and $x_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}$ are adjacent if and only if $i\neq i^{\prime}$ . We call this set of vertices the base vertices, because we continue to add vertices to $G$ . Let $X_{i}=\{x_{i,j}\mid 1\leq j\leq k\}$ be the set corresponding to the vertex $v_{i}$ in $V(H)$ . The partition $\mathfrak{X}$ starts as the set $\{X_{1},\dots,X_{n}\}$ . We add vertices to these sets, as we continue to construct $G$ in the following three steps:

- (1) For every $v_{i}v_{j}\in E(H)$ , add two new vertices $z_{j,i}$ and $z_{i,j}$ to $V(G)$ . Add the edges from $z_{j,i}$ , $z_{i,j}$ to all base vertices except those in $X_{i}$ and $X_{j}$ . Assign the vertex $z_{j,i}$ to $X_{j}$ and the vertex $z_{i,j}$ to $X_{i}$ . Note that any vertex $z_{a,b}$ lives in $X_{a}$ .

- (2) For every $v_{i}v_{j}\notin E(H)$ , add one new vertex $w_{i,j}$ to $V(G)$ . Since both $v_{i}$ and $v_{j}$ have degree at least $1$ and are not adjacent to each other, there exists at least one other vertex $v_{l}\in H^{\prime}$ , with a corresponding set $X_{l}$ . Add the edges from $w_{i,j}$ to all base vertices except those in $X_{i}$ , $X_{j}$ , and $X_{l}$ . Assign the vertex $w_{i,j}$ to $X_{l}$ .

- (3) If $u_{i}$ is an isolated vertex in $H$ , then the corresponding set in $\mathfrak{X}$ must be a $k$ -dominating set with exactly $k$ -vertices (so that it does not form a $k$ -coalition with any other set). Take the complete graph $K_{mk}$ , with vertex set $\{y_{i,1},\dots,y_{i,k}\mid 1\leq i\leq m\}$ , and graph join $K_{mk}$ and $V(G)$ . Then we partition the vertices into sets. For every $1\leq i\leq m$ , add the set $Y_{i}=\{y_{i,1},\dots,y_{i,k}\}$ to $\mathfrak{X}$ .

Set $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{n}\}\cup\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{m}\}$ . Each set $X_{i}$ corresponds to the vertex $v_{i}$ and every set $Y_{i}$ corresponds to the vertex $u_{i}$ . We first verify that $\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition of $G$ . Every set $Y_{i}\in\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -dominating set of $G$ with $k$ vertices. Since $\deg(v_{i})\geq 1$ , each vertex $v_{i}$ must be adjacent to at least one vertex $v_{j}$ , where $i\neq j$ . We check that $X_{i}$ and $X_{j}$ form a $k$ -coalition. The sets $X_{i}$ and $X_{j}$ are not $k$ -dominating sets because $X_{i}$ does not $k$ -dominate $z_{j,i}$ and $X_{j}$ does not $k$ -dominate $z_{i,j}$ . Moreover, all the base vertices in $V(G)\setminus(X_{i}\cup X_{j})$ are adjacent to the base vertices in $X_{i}$ and $X_{j}$ . For any edge $v_{k}v_{l}\in E(H)\setminus\{v_{i}v_{j}\}$ , the two added vertices $z_{k,l}$ and $z_{l,k}$ are adjacent to the base vertices in $X_{i}$ , $X_{j}$ , or both. Similarly, for any non-edge $v_{k}v_{l}$ , the added vertex $w_{k,l}$ is adjacent to the base vertices of $X_{i}$ or $X_{j}$ , or $w_{k,l}$ is contained in one of the two sets. Since all vertices in $G\setminus(X_{i}\cup X_{j})$ are adjacent to the base vertices in $X_{i}\cup X_{j}$ , we have that $X_{i}\cup X_{j}$ $k$ -dominates $G$ . Therefore, $X_{i}$ and $X_{j}$ form a $k$ -coalition.

Lastly, we observe that $\operatorname{kCG}(\mathfrak{X},G)=H$ . Every isolated vertex $w_{i}\in V(G)$ corresponds to the set $Y_{i}\in\mathfrak{X}$ and $Y_{i}$ is a $k$ -dominating set of $H$ with $k$ vertices. Therefore, $Y_{i}$ does not have any $k$ -coalition partners in $\mathfrak{X}$ . If $v_{i}v_{j}\in E(H)$ , then, by the argument above, $X_{i}$ and $X_{j}$ form a $k$ -coalition. If $v_{i}v_{j}\notin E(H)$ , then there exists a vertex $w_{i,j}$ that is not adjacent to any vertex in $X_{i}$ or $X_{j}$ . Therefore, $X_{i}\cup X_{j}$ does not $k$ -dominate $w_{i,j}$ and are not $k$ -coalition partners. ∎

## Appendix A Proof of Theorem 3.11

Before presenting the main argument, we prove several useful lemmas. We first establish a general lower bound on the $k$ -coalition number, which is shown to be optimal in certain cases, particularly when $k$ is close to $s_{1}$ .

#### Lemma A.1.

Fix $k\geq 2$ . For every $K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}}$ with $k<s_{1}$ it follows that

$$ \COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})\geq\left(\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}\right)-k+3. $$

#### Proof.

It is sufficient to construct a $k$ -coalition partition with exactly $(\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i})-k+3$ sets. For every $1\leq i\leq r$ , label the vertices of $S_{i}$ as $\{v_{i,1},v_{i,2},\dots,v_{i,s_{i}}\}$ . Define $X_{1}\subseteq S_{1}\cup S_{2}$ and $X_{2}\subseteq S_{1}$ as follows:

$$ \displaystyle X_{1}=\{v_{1,1},v_{1,2},\dots,v_{1,k}\}\cup\{v_{2,1},v_{2,2},\dots,v_{2,k-1}\}; \displaystyle X_{2}=\{v_{1,k+1},\dots,v_{1,s_{1}}\}. $$

Set

$$ \mathfrak{X}=\left\{X_{1},X_{2}\right\}\cup\left\{\{v\}\mid v\in V(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})\setminus(X_{1}\cup X_{2})\right\}. $$

The partition $\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition, where every set is a singleton except $X_{1}$ and possibly $X_{2}$ . Indeed, no set is individually a $k$ -dominating set, but $X_{1}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with every set in $\mathfrak{X}$ . See Figure 8 for an example. We deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})\geq|V|-|X_{1}\cup X_{2}|+2=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}\right)-(s_{1}+k-1)+2=\left(\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}\right)-k+3.\quad\quad\qed $$

#### Lemma A.2.

Fix $k\geq 2$ and $k<s_{1}$ . Let $D$ be a $k$ -dominating set of $K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}}$ . Suppose that $D$ intersects $m$ partite sets and $D$ does not contain any partite set (entirely). Then

$$ |D|\geq k+\left\lceil\frac{k}{m-1}\right\rceil. $$

#### Proof.

Suppose that $D$ intersects the partite set $S_{i}$ . Since $D$ does not contain $S_{i}$ , there exist vertices in $S_{i}$ that are not in $D$ . To $k$ -dominate these vertices, it must be that $|D\cap(V\setminus S_{i})|\geq k$ . Therefore, it follows that $m\geq 2$ . By the pigeonhole principle, there exists at least one partite set $S_{j}$ such that $|D\cap S_{j}|\geq\lceil\frac{k}{m-1}\rceil$ . Since $D$ also does not contain $S_{j}$ , to $k$ -dominate the vertices in $S_{j}\cap(V\setminus D)$ , we have $|D\cap(V\setminus S_{j})|\geq k$ . Thus,

$$ |D|=|D\cap(V\setminus S_{j})|+|D\cap S_{j}|\geq k+\left\lceil\frac{k}{m-1}\right\rceil.\qed $$

#### Lemma A.3.

There are no $k$ -dominating sets of $K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}}$ with exactly $k$ vertices.

#### Proof.

Let $D$ be a $k$ -dominating set of $K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}}$ . If $D$ contains an entire partite set $S_{i}$ , then $|D|\geq s_{i}\geq s_{1}>k$ , as required. We may now assume there exists at least one vertex $v\in S_{1}\cap(V\setminus D)$ . To $k$ -dominate $v$ , the set $D$ must include vertices from $V(G)\setminus S_{1}$ , implying that $D$ intersects at least two sets. By Lemma A.2, with $m\geq 2$ ,

$$ |D|\geq k+\left\lceil\frac{k}{m-1}\right\rceil\geq k+1.\qed $$

#### Lemma A.4.

Suppose $r\geq 3$ . Let $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{\COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})}\}$ be a $k$ -coalition partition of $K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}}$ with the maximum number of sets. Then $\mathfrak{X}$ contains at least one singleton set.

#### Proof.

We proceed by contradiction. Suppose that $|X_{i}|\geq 2$ for all $X_{i}\in\mathfrak{X}$ . By Lemma A.3, $K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}}$ has no $k$ -dominating sets of size $k$ . Therefore, there exist at least two sets $X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathfrak{X}$ that form a $k$ -coalition and $|X_{1}\cup X_{2}|>k$ . Since all other sets in $\mathfrak{X}$ consist of at least two vertices, it follows that

$$ |\mathfrak{X}|<\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i})-k}{2}+2\leq\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-k)+(\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-s_{1}-k)}{2}+2=\left(\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}\right)-k+2, $$

where the second inequality follows from the observation that $\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-s_{1}-k\geq 0$ when $r\geq 3$ . However, by Lemma A.1, $\COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})\geq\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-k+3$ . Therefore, $\mathfrak{X}$ is not a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition, a contradiction. ∎

#### Lemma A.5.

Let $\mathfrak{X}$ be a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition of $K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}}$ . If $\mathfrak{X}$ has $k$ -coalition partners $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ such that $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ contains an entire partite set, then $\COk(G)\leq\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-k+3$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose that $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{\COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})}\}$ is such a $k$ -coalition partition and $S_{j}\subseteq X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ . Note that neither $X_{1}$ nor $X_{2}$ can individually contain the entire partite set $S_{j}$ , since then they would then be $k$ -dominating. If $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ , then $\COk(G)=2$ and we are done. We may assume there exists another set $X_{3}\in\mathfrak{X}$ . By Observation 3.1, $X_{3}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set, and therefore has a $k$ -coalition partner, $X_{4}$ . By Lemma A.3, we have $|X_{3}\cup X_{4}|\geq k+1$ . If $X_{4}\notin\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ , then

$$ |\mathfrak{X}|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-|X_{1}\cup X_{2}|-|X_{3}\cup X_{4}|+4\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-s_{j}-(k+1)+4\leq\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-k+3, $$

where the last inequality follows from the fact that $s_{j}\geq s_{1}$ . If $X_{4}\in\{X_{1},X_{2}\}$ , suppose without loss of generality that $X_{4}=X_{2}$ . In order to $k$ -dominate the vertices in $X_{1}\cap S_{j}$ , we have $|(X_{2}\cup X_{3})\cap(V(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})\setminus S_{j})|\geq k$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle|\mathfrak{X}| \displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-|X_{1}\cup X_{2}\cup X_{3}|+3\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-s_{j}-k+3\leq\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-k+3.\qed $$

#### Lemma A.6.

Suppose $k\geq r$ and $r>1$ , then $k+\big\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\big\rceil-1\not\equiv 0\pmod{r}$ .

#### Proof.

Write $k=q(r-1)+d$ for some $q\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $0\leq d<r-1$ . First, suppose $d=0$ . Then

$$ k+\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil-1=q(r-1)+q-1=qr-1\not\equiv 0\pmod{r}. $$

Next, suppose $1\leq d<r-1$ . Then $\big\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\big\rceil=\big\lceil q+\frac{d}{r-1}\big\rceil=q+1$ , and so

$$ k+\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil-1=(q(r-1)+d)+(q+1)-1=qr+d\not\equiv 0\pmod{r}.\qed $$

We now have the tools required to prove the main theorem.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.11.

We proceed by casework.

We may now assume $k\geq 2$ . Let $\mathfrak{X}=\{X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{\COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})}\}$ be a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition of $\COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})$ . By Lemma A.4, there is at least one singleton set $X_{1}\in\mathfrak{X}$ , which must have at least one coalition partner $X_{2}\in\mathfrak{X}$ . By Lemma A.3, $|X_{1}\cup X_{2}|\geq k+1$ , and consequently $|X_{2}|\geq k$ .

(1) If $X_{2}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with every set in $\mathfrak{X}$ , then $|\mathfrak{X}|\leq\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-k+3$ .

By Lemma 3.4, the set $X_{2}$ has at most $\Delta(G)-k+2$ distinct $k$ -coalition partners. Since $\Delta(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})=\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}$ , it follows that $|\mathfrak{X}|\leq 1+\Delta(G)-k+2=\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-k+3$ , which proves (A).

Now suppose there exists some set $X_{3}\in\mathfrak{X}$ that does not form a $k$ -coalition with $X_{2}$ . By Lemma A.3, the set $X_{3}$ cannot be a $k$ -dominating set itself, and so it has a $k$ -coalition partner $X_{t}$ , where $t\notin\{2,3\}$ . In particular, it is possible that $t=1$ . By Lemma A.5, if $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ or $X_{3}\cup X_{t}$ contains an entire partite set, then $|\mathfrak{X}|\leq\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-k+3$ .

Since we lower bound the $k$ -coalition number with the construction in Lemma A.1, if the maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition has a structure as described above, then the $k$ -coalition number is equal to $\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-k+3$ . However, these cases are only optimal when $s_{1}$ is close in size to $k$ .

We now examine the cases where the maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition does not admit this structure and the $k$ -coalition number will exceed this lower bound. Label the vertices of the partite set $S_{i}$ as $v_{i,1},v_{i,2},\dots,v_{i,s_{i}}$ . Note that $|X_{2}|\geq k$ and $|X_{3}\cup X_{t}|\geq k+1$ . We now suppose that neither $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ nor $X_{3}\cup X_{t}$ contains a partite set and consider the following cases:

(2) If $r\geq 2k$ , then $\COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})=\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k+2$ .

Upper Bound. Note that $|V\setminus(X_{2}\cup X_{3}\cup X_{t})|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-k-(k+1)$ . We may upper bound the number of sets in $\mathfrak{X}$ by assuming that all other sets are singletons. Hence

$$ \COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})=|\mathfrak{X}|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-1+3=\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k+2. $$

Lower Bound. Let $Y_{1}=\{v_{1,1},v_{2,1},\dots,v_{k,1}\}$ and $Y_{2}=\{v_{k+1,1},v_{k+2,1},\dots,v_{2k,1}\}$ . Then the following is a $k$ -coalition partition of $K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}}$ :

$$ \mathfrak{X}=\left\{Y_{1},Y_{2}\right\}\cup\left\{\{v\}\mid v\in V\setminus(Y_{1}\cup Y_{2})\right\}. $$

See Figure 9 (left) for an example. The set $Y_{1}$ contains one vertex from each of $S_{1},\dots,S_{k}$ and the set $Y_{2}$ contains one vertex from each of $S_{k+1},\dots,S_{2k}$ . We take the remaining vertices to be singleton sets. Then $Y_{1}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with every singleton $\{v\}$ where $v\in V\setminus(S_{1}\cup\dots\cup S_{k})$ and $Y_{2}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with every singleton $\{v\}$ where $v\in V\setminus(S_{k+1}\cup\dots\cup S_{2k})$ . Consequently, $\COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})\geq\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k+2,$ which proves (A).

(3) If $k<r<2k$ , then $\COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})=\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k+1$ .

Upper Bound. First, suppose that $|X_{1}\cup X_{2}|>k+1$ (implying that $|X_{2}|>k$ ) or $|X_{3}\cup X_{t}|>k+1$ . Then, even if all the other sets in $\mathfrak{X}$ are singleton sets, it follows that

$$ |\mathfrak{X}|\leq|V\setminus(X_{2}\cup X_{3}\cup X_{t})|+3<\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-1+3=\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k+2. $$

Now assume that $|X_{1}\cup X_{2}|=k+1$ (so, in particular, $|X_{2}|=k$ ) and $|X_{3}\cup X_{t}|=k+1$ . For contradiction, suppose that all sets in $\mathfrak{X}\setminus\{X_{2},X_{3},X_{t}\}$ are singletons. We will argue that this is not possible.

Note that every partite set has at least $3$ vertices, and by Lemma A.3 every $k$ -dominating set has at least $3$ vertices. Therefore no two singleton sets can form a $k$ -coalition. By assumption, neither $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ nor $X_{3}\cup X_{t}$ contains an entire partite set, so Lemma A.2 implies that the $k$ -dominating sets $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ and $X_{3}\cup X_{t}$ must each intersect $k+1$ partite sets, with one vertex from each.

If $X_{2}$ intersects the partite set $S_{j}$ , then there exists at least one vertex $v\in S_{j}\setminus(X_{2}\cup X_{3}\cup X_{t})$ . By assumption, $\{v\}$ is a singleton set in $\mathfrak{X}$ . However, $X_{2}\cup\{v\}$ is not a $k$ -dominating set because it does not $k$ -dominate the remaining vertices in $S_{j}\setminus(X_{2}\cup\{v\})$ . If both $|X_{3}|<k$ and $|X_{t}|<k$ , then neither $X_{3}$ nor $X_{t}$ has enough vertices to form a $k$ -coalition with $\{v\}$ . Hence, $\{v\}$ does not have a $k$ -coalition partner, a contradiction.

Hence, either $X_{3}$ or $X_{t}$ has exactly $k$ vertices. Without loss of generality, say $|X_{3}|=k$ and $|X_{t}|=1$ . Then, since $X_{2}$ and $X_{3}$ each intersect $k$ distinct partite sets and there are at most $2k-1$ partite sets, there is some partite set $S_{l}$ intersecting both $X_{2}$ and $X_{3}$ . Since $S_{l}$ has at least three vertices, there is at least one vertex $u\in S_{l}\setminus(X_{2}\cup X_{3})$ . However, $\{u\}$ does not form a $k$ -coalition with $X_{2}$ or $X_{3}$ , since $\{u\}\cup X_{3}$ does not $k$ -dominate the vertices in $X_{2}\cap S_{l}$ . Similarly $\{u\}\cup X_{2}$ does not $k$ -dominate the vertices in $X_{3}\cap S_{l}$ . Therefore, $\{u\}$ does not have a $k$ -coalition partner, a contradiction.

Since there is at least one set in $\mathfrak{X}\setminus\{X_{2},X_{3},X_{t}\}$ that is not a singleton set, we have the bound

$$ |\mathfrak{X}|<|V\setminus(X_{2}\cup X_{3}\cup X_{t})|+3\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-1+3=\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k+2. $$

Lower Bound. If $s_{1}\leq k+2$ , then $\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k+1\leq\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-k+3$ and the construction in Lemma A.1 achieves the maximum. We assume here that $s_{1}\geq k+2$ . Let $Y_{1}=\{v_{1,1},v_{2,1},\dots,v_{k,1}\}$ and $Y_{2}=\{v_{2,2},\dots,v_{k+1,2}\}\cup\{v_{k+1,1}\}$ . Then define

$$ \mathfrak{X}=\left\{Y_{1},Y_{2}\right\}\cup\left\{\{v\}\mid v\in V\setminus(Y_{1}\cup Y_{2})\right\}. $$

See Figure 9 (right) for this construction. The set $Y_{1}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with every singleton in $S_{i}$ where $i\geq k+1$ and $Y_{2}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with every singleton in $S_{i}$ when $i\neq k+1$ . Hence, $\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition. Therefore,

$$ |\mathfrak{X}|\geq\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-k-(k+1)+2=\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k+1. $$

(4) If $r\leq k$ and $k+\big\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\big\rceil-1\pmod{r}\leq\frac{r}{2}$ , then

$$ \COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})=\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-2\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil+4. $$

Upper Bound. Since the $k$ -dominating sets $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ and $X_{3}\cup X_{t}$ each intersect at most $k$ partite sets, Lemma A.2 implies that $|X_{1}\cup X_{2}|\geq k+\big\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\big\rceil$ and $|X_{3}\cup X_{t}|\geq k+\big\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\big\rceil$ . By assuming all other sets in the partition are singleton sets, we obtain the bound

$$ |\mathfrak{X}|\geq|V\setminus(X_{2}\cup X_{3}\cup X_{t})|+3=\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-2\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil+4. $$

Lower Bound. When $s_{1}\leq k+2\big\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\big\rceil-1$ , we have

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-2\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil+4\leq\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-k+3. $$

In this case, the construction in Lemma A.1 is a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition. In what follows, we assume that $s_{1}\geq k+2\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil-1$ . Set $m=k+\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil-1\pmod{r}$ and $n=\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ . By Lemma A.6, $0<m\leq\frac{r}{2}$ and, by assumption, $s_{i}\geq 2n-1$ for all $i$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle Y_{1}=\{v_{i,1},\dots,v_{i,n}\mid 1\leq i\leq m\}\cup\{v_{i,1},\dots,v_{i,n-1}\mid m+1\leq i\leq r\}; \displaystyle Y_{2}=\{v_{i,n+1},\dots,v_{i,2n-1}\mid 1\leq i\leq r-m\}\cup\{v_{i,n},\dots,v_{i,2n-1}\mid r-m+1\leq i\leq r\}. $$

Then set

$$ \mathfrak{X}=\left\{Y_{1},Y_{2}\right\}\cup\left\{\{v\}\mid v\in V\setminus(Y_{1}\cup Y_{2})\right\}. $$

See Figure 10 for this construction. Then $Y_{1}$ and $Y_{2}$ are not $k$ -dominating sets because $Y_{1}$ does not $k$ -dominate the vertices in $(S_{1}\cup\dots\cup S_{m})\setminus Y_{1}$ and $Y_{2}$ does not $k$ -dominate the vertices in $(S_{r-m+1}\cup\dots\cup S_{r})\setminus Y_{2}$ . Moreover, $Y_{1}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with every singleton in $S_{m+1},S_{m+2},\dots,S_{r}$ (where $m+1\leq\frac{r}{2}+1$ ) and $Y_{2}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with every singleton in $S_{1},S_{2},\dots,S_{r-m}$ (where $r-m\geq\frac{r}{2})$ . Hence, $\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition and we have

$$ \displaystyle|\mathfrak{X}|\geq|V\setminus(Y_{1}\cup Y_{2})|+2\geq\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-2\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil+4, $$

which proves (A). Note that complete bipartite graphs fall under (A) and our results agree with Theorem 3.10 [6].

(5) If $r\leq k$ and $k+\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil-1\pmod{r}>\frac{r}{2}$ , then

$$ \COk(K_{s_{1},\dots,s_{r}})=\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-2\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil+3. $$

Upper Bound. For every $r\geq 3$ , when $s_{1}\leq k+2\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ , we have

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-2\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil\leq\sum_{i=2}^{r}s_{i}-k+3. $$

In this case, the construction from Lemma A.1 is a maximum-size $k$ -coalition partition. We may now assume $s_{1}\geq k+2\big\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\big\rceil$ . As above, $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ and $X_{3}\cup X_{t}$ each intersect at most $r$ partite sets (and do not contain an entire partite set), so Lemma A.2 implies both $|X_{1}\cup X_{2}|\geq k+\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ and $|X_{3}\cup X_{t}|\geq k+\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ . If $|X_{1}\cup X_{2}|>k+\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ or $|X_{3}\cup X_{t}|>k+\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ , then

$$ |\mathfrak{X}|\leq|V\setminus(X_{2}\cup X_{3}\cup X_{t})|+3<\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-2\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil+4. $$

We now assume $|X_{1}\cup X_{2}|=k+\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ and $|X_{3}\cup X_{t}|=k+\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ . For contradiction, suppose that all the remaining sets in $\mathfrak{X}\setminus\{X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},X_{t}\}$ are singletons. Since no pair of singletons can form a $k$ -coalition, we obtain the contradiction by finding at least one singleton set that cannot form a $k$ -coalition with $X_{2},X_{3},$ or $X_{t}$ .

By Lemma A.2, the $k$ -dominating sets $X_{1}\cup X_{2}$ and $X_{3}\cup X_{t}$ must each intersect all $r$ partite sets, with at most $\big\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\big\rceil$ vertices per partite set. Since $s_{j}\geq s_{1}\geq k+2\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ , we have $|S_{j}\setminus\{X_{2},X_{3},X_{t}\}|\geq k$ and so every partite set $S_{j}$ has at least two vertices $u,v$ that are not in $X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}$ or $X_{t}$ .

Let $m=k+\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil-1\pmod{r}$ . By a counting argument, there are $m$ partite sets $S_{j}$ such that $|X_{2}\cap S_{j}|=\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ vertices. Suppose that $|X_{3}|\geq|X_{t}|$ (the case where $|X_{3}|\leq|X_{t}|$ follows by a symmetric argument). If $|X_{3}|<k+\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil-1$ , then $X_{t}$ and $X_{3}$ do not have enough vertices to form a $k$ -coalition with a singleton. If $|X_{3}|=k+\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil-1$ (so $|X_{t}|=1$ ), then there are $m$ distinct partite sets $S_{j}$ such that $|X_{3}\cap S_{j}|=\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ . Since $m>\frac{r}{2}$ , there is at least one partite set $S_{j}$ such that both $|X_{2}\cap S_{j}|=\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ and $|X_{3}\cap S_{j}|=\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ . Then

$$ |X_{2}\cap(V\setminus S_{j})|\leq|X_{2}|-|X_{2}\cap S_{j}|\leq k-1\quad\text{and}\quad|X_{3}\cap(V\setminus S_{j})|\leq|X_{3}|-|X_{3}\cap S_{j}|\leq k-1. $$

Consequently, $X_{2}$ and $X_{3}$ do not $k$ -dominate $u$ and $v$ . Since $u$ and $v$ are non-adjacent, neither $X_{2}\cup\{v\}$ nor $X_{3}\cup\{v\}$ can $k$ -dominate $u$ . Therefore, the singleton set $\{v\}$ does not form a $k$ -coalition with $X_{2}$ , $X_{3}$ , or $X_{t}$ . We conclude that there is at least one set in $\mathfrak{X}\setminus\{X_{2},X_{3},X_{t}\}$ that is not a singleton set. Therefore

$$ |\mathfrak{X}|<|V\setminus(X_{2}\cup X_{3}\cup X_{t})|+3=\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-2\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil+4. $$

Lower Bound. Let $n=\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\rceil$ and recall that $m>\frac{r}{2}$ . Set

$$ \displaystyle Y_{1}=\{v_{i,1},\dots,v_{i,n}\mid 1\leq i\leq m\}\cup\{v_{i,1},\dots,v_{i,n-1}\mid m+1\leq i\leq r\}; \displaystyle Y_{2}=\{v_{i,n+1},\dots,v_{i,2n-1}\mid 1\leq i\leq r-m\}\cup\{v_{i,n+1},\dots,v_{i,2n}\mid r-m+1\leq i\leq r\}\cup\{v_{r,n}\}. $$

Define

$$ \mathfrak{X}=\left\{Y_{1},Y_{2}\right\}\cup\left\{\{v\}\mid v\in V\setminus(Y_{1}\cup Y_{2})\right\}. $$

Note that $Y_{1}$ and $Y_{2}$ are not $k$ -dominating sets because $Y_{1}$ does not $k$ -dominate any vertex in $(S_{1}\cup\dots\cup S_{m})\setminus Y_{1}$ and $Y_{2}$ does not $k$ -dominate any vertex in $S_{r}\setminus Y_{2}$ . Since $1<m<r$ , the set $Y_{1}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with each singleton $\{v\}$ in $S_{r}$ , and the set $Y_{2}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with each singleton $\{v\}$ in $S_{1}\cup S_{2}\cup\dots\cup S_{r-1}$ . Every singleton in $\mathfrak{X}$ forms a $k$ -coalition with $Y_{1}$ or $Y_{2}$ . Hence, $\mathfrak{X}$ is a $k$ -coalition partition and we have

$$ |\mathfrak{X}|\geq|V\setminus(Y_{1}\cup Y_{2})|+2\geq\sum_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}-2k-2\left\lceil\frac{k}{r-1}\right\rceil+3, $$

which proves (A). ∎
